claim: The bx1 mutant exhibits a strong reduction in benzoxazinoid production due to a transposon insertion in the Bx1 gene.
source: Compared to its wild type counterpart, the bx1 mutant exhibits a strong reduction in benzoxazinoid production due to a transposon insertion in the Bx1 gene (Tzin et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tzin et al., 2015, which provides external evidence for the genetic basis of the bx1 mutant phenotype.

claim: Consistent soil conditioning and feedback effects can be triggered by different bx1 mutant alleles in different genetic backgrounds.
source: Previous work has shown that consistent soil conditioning and feedback effects can be triggered by different bx1 mutant alleles in different genetic backgrounds (Hu et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hu et al., 2018b, which provides evidence from prior research.

claim: Wild type and bx1 mutant maize plants grew similarly and accumulated the same amount of biomass at the end of the growing season.
source: Both maize genotypes grew similarly and accumulated the same amount of biomass at the end of the growing season, most likely due to abundant micronutrients and low pest pressure (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, which shows experimental data on maize biomass.

claim: Substantial amounts of benzoxazinoids and benzoxazinoid degradation products were detected in the soils of plots cultivated with wild-type plants.
source: Substantial amounts of benzoxazinoids and benzoxazinoid degradation products were detected in the soils of plots cultivated with wild-type plants (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A, which presents experimental measurements of benzoxazinoid concentrations.

claim: HDMBOA-Glc was the most abundant benzoxazinoid in wild-type conditioned soil.
source: HDMBOA-Glc was the most abundant benzoxazinoid, followed by HMBOA, DIMBOA, and DIMBOA-Glc.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of benzoxazinoid measurements in the text and Figure 1A.

claim: Most benzoxazinoids were below the limit of detection in the soils planted with bx1 mutant plants.
source: Most benzoxazinoids were below the limit of detection in the soils planted with bx1 mutant plants, indicating that concentrations of the highly emitted compounds (e.g. HDMBOA-Glc) were more than 100 times lower in bx1 mutant compared to wild type conditioned soil.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements described in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Concentrations of highly emitted benzoxazinoids were more than 100 times lower in bx1 mutant compared to wild type conditioned soil.
source: Most benzoxazinoids were below the limit of detection in the soils planted with bx1 mutant plants, indicating that concentrations of the highly emitted compounds (e.g. HDMBOA-Glc) were more than 100 times lower in bx1 mutant compared to wild type conditioned soil.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from detection limits and comparative measurements between wild type and bx1 mutant soils.

claim: Most benzoxazinoids were 3- to 800-fold less abundant 6 weeks after maize harvest than at the end of maize cultivation.
source: Most benzoxazinoids were 3- to 800-fold less abundant than at the end of maize cultivation (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of benzoxazinoid concentrations at two time points, as shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: Concentrations of AMPO increased more than twofold 6 weeks after maize harvest.
source: Concentrations of the stable breakdown product AMPO increased more than twofold.
evidence: The claim is supported by benzoxazinoid measurements comparing time points, as shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: DIMBOA, HMBOA, MBOA and AMPO were present in higher concentrations in wild type conditioned soils 6 weeks after maize harvest.
source: DIMBOA, HMBOA, MBOA and AMPO were present in higher concentrations in wild type conditioned soils.
evidence: The claim is supported by benzoxazinoid measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Only trace levels of DIMBOA-Glc and HDMBOA-Glc were found 6 weeks after maize harvest, and their concentrations were higher in bx1 mutant conditioned soils.
source: Only trace levels of the two glycosylated benzoxazinoids, DIMBOA-Glc and HDMBOA-Glc were found, and their concentrations were higher in bx1 mutant conditioned soils.
evidence: The claim is supported by benzoxazinoid measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Higher concentrations of glycosylated benzoxazinoids in bx1 mutant conditioned soils indicate faster deglycosylation in wild type conditioned soils.
source: As benzoxazinoids are released as glycosides and deglycosylated in the soil, this result is indicative of faster deglycosylation in wild type conditioned soils.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that glycosylated forms are higher in bx1 soils, combined with knowledge about benzoxazinoid metabolism.

claim: No significant differences in soil macro and micronutrient levels and pH were found between soils cultivated with wild type or bx1 mutant plants at the end of maize cultivation.
source: No significant differences were found between soils cultivated with wild type or bx1 mutant plants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by soil nutrient analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: HDMBOA-Glc, HMBOA, and MBOA differences were not detected during wheat growth.
source: The previous differences in benzoxazinoid levels of HDMBOA-Glc, HMBOA, and MBOA were not detected any more at this point, and DIMBOA-Glc was no longer detected at all (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by benzoxazinoid measurements during wheat growth shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DIMBOA-Glc was no longer detected during wheat growth.
source: The previous differences in benzoxazinoid levels of HDMBOA-Glc, HMBOA, and MBOA were not detected any more at this point, and DIMBOA-Glc was no longer detected at all (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by benzoxazinoid measurements during wheat growth shown in Figure 1C.

claim: AMPO levels were significantly and consistently higher in plots conditioned with wild type maize across all three wheat varieties during wheat growth.
source: However, AMPO levels were still significantly and consistently higher in plots conditioned with wild type maize across all three wheat varieties.
evidence: The claim is supported by benzoxazinoid measurements during wheat growth shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Modulating benzoxazinoid production results in a persistent soil chemical fingerprint that is still present in the next crop generation.
source: Taken together, these results show that modulating benzoxazinoid production results in a persistent soil chemical fingerprint that is still present in the next crop generation, even if the next crop also produces benzoxazinoids.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that AMPO levels remain elevated during wheat growth, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The biggest taxonomic differences at the phylum level were found between the three compartments: root, rhizosphere, and soil at maize harvest.
source: At maize harvest, the biggest taxonomic differences at the phylum level were found between the three compartments: root, rhizosphere, and soil (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microbial community analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PERMANOVA on Bray-Curtis distances revealed significant differences between genotypes in bacterial and fungal community composition of roots and rhizosphere after taking the effect of the sequencing run into account.
source: Permutational Multivariate Analysis of Variance (PERMANOVA) on Bray-Curtis distances revealed significant differences between genotypes in bacterial and fungal community composition of roots and rhizosphere after taking the effect of the sequencing run into account (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of microbial community data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 9.7% to 15.7% of the total variation within compartments was explained by the maize genotype.
source: 9.7 % to 15.7 % of the total variation within compartments was explained by the maize genotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by PERMANOVA analysis results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The benzoxazinoid effect on bacterial and fungal communities was comparable in the roots (R2 bacteria = 13%, R2 fungi = 12.7%).
source: The benzoxazinoid effect on bacterial and fungal communities was comparable in the roots (R2 bacteria = 13 %, R2 fungi = 12.7 %).
evidence: The claim is supported by PERMANOVA analysis results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the rhizosphere, a more pronounced effect on the fungal community relative to the bacterial community was found (bacteria = 9.7%, fungi = 15.7%).
source: In the rhizosphere, we found a more pronounced effect on the fungal community relative to the bacterial community (bacteria = 9.7 %, fungi = 15.7 %).
evidence: The claim is supported by PERMANOVA analysis results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No benzoxazinoid effects were detected in bulk soil microbial communities at maize harvest.
source: In bulk soil, no benzoxazinoid effects were detected (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by PERMANOVA analysis results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Visualization of bacterial and fungal communities by CAP showed a clear differentiation between maize genotypes in the roots and rhizosphere.
source: In line with PERMANOVA, visualization of bacterial and fungal communities by Constrained Analysis of Principal Coordinates (CAP) showed a clear differentiation between maize genotypes in the roots and rhizosphere (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by CAP analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Benzoxazinoids structure root-associated microbial communities in maize.
source: Overall, these results confirm that benzoxazinoids structure root-associated microbial communities in maize.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the PERMANOVA and CAP analyses showing genotype effects on microbial communities.

claim: The strongest taxonomic differences at phylum level during wheat maturation were found between compartments.
source: Again, the strongest taxonomic differences at phylum level were found between compartments (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by microbial community analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: PERMANOVA revealed a consistent difference in community composition between wheat varieties, with Sailor being the most dissimilar to the others.
source: PERMANOVA revealed a consistent difference in community composition between wheat varieties, with Sailor being the most dissimilar to the others (Figure 2C/D).
evidence: The claim is supported by PERMANOVA analysis results shown in Figure 2C/D.

claim: PERMANOVA did not reveal any benzoxazinoid-dependent effects on microbial community composition during wheat maturation.
source: PERMANOVA did not reveal any benzoxazinoid-dependent effects on microbial community composition.
evidence: The claim is supported by PERMANOVA analysis results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was no clear legacy effect on microbial community composition at the onset of wheat maturation.
source: Thus, there was no clear legacy effect on microbial community composition at the onset of wheat maturation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the lack of benzoxazinoid-dependent effects in PERMANOVA analysis.

claim: Overall, wheat seedling emergence was increased by 8% in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils.
source: Overall, wheat seedling emergence was increased by 8% in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by seedling emergence measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Chlorophyll content measured in the youngest fully developed leaf was increased in plants growing in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils.
source: Chlorophyll content measured in the youngest fully developed leaf (as a proxy for early plant performance) was also increased in plants growing in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by chlorophyll measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Wheat growth, height, and biomass production per area were enhanced in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils.
source: Wheat growth, height, and biomass production per area, as well as shoot water content were also enhanced (Figure 3C/D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by plant growth measurements shown in Figures 3C/D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Shoot water content was enhanced in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils.
source: Wheat growth, height, and biomass production per area, as well as shoot water content were also enhanced (Figure 3C/D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by shoot water content measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Benzoxazinoid soil conditioning increases wheat performance across different wheat varieties.
source: Thus, benzoxazinoid soil conditioning increases wheat performance across different wheat varieties.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the consistent positive effects observed across multiple wheat varieties in Figures 3A-D.

claim: Weed pressure differed along the field.
source: We found that weed pressure differed along the field, and therefore accounted for positional effects in the analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by weed cover measurements and statistical analysis accounting for position.

claim: No effect of soil conditioning status on weed abundance was found for the varieties Claro and Fiorina.
source: We found no effect of soil conditioning status on weed abundance for the varieties Claro and Fiorina (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by weed cover measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No weeds were detected with the variety Sailor due to herbicide treatment.
source: No weeds were detected with the variety Sailor, as this variety was treated with herbicides.
evidence: The claim is supported by weed cover measurements shown in Figure 4A and knowledge of the herbicide treatment.

claim: The abundance of Oulema larvae was significantly reduced on wheat plants of all three varieties grown in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils.
source: The abundance of Oulema larvae was significantly reduced on wheat plants of all three varieties grown in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils, with the biggest difference in the variety Sailor (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by insect abundance measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The biggest difference in Oulema larvae abundance was in the variety Sailor.
source: The abundance of Oulema larvae was significantly reduced on wheat plants of all three varieties grown in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils, with the biggest difference in the variety Sailor (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by insect abundance measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No clear effect was found in terms of insect damage, apart from a tendency of decreased damage on Sailor.
source: No clear effect was found in terms of insect damage, apart from a tendency of decreased damage on Sailor (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by leaf damage measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: No significant influence of benzoxazinoid soil conditioning was found on defense hormone levels.
source: No significant influence of benzoxazinoid soil conditioning was found (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phytohormone measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: All wheat varieties had a higher number of tillers per area in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils.
source: All wheat varieties had a higher number of tillers per area in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by tiller density measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Plants in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils produced a higher number of tillers per plant.
source: Overall, plants in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils produced a higher numbers of tillers per plant.
evidence: The claim is supported by tiller per plant measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The pattern of increased tillers per plant was consistent across all varieties, with the most pronounced difference in the variety Sailor.
source: This pattern was consistent across all varieties, with the most pronounced difference in the variety Sailor (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by tiller per plant measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Benzoxazinoid soil conditioning increased biomass at plant maturity.
source: Consistent with the results during wheat growth, benzoxazinoid soil conditioning also increased biomass at plant maturity (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by biomass measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The weight of individual tillers was similar between soil conditioning treatments.
source: The weight of individual tillers was similar (Figure 5D), demonstrating that benzoxazinoid soil conditioning increased biomass by promoting tiller density, both through enhanced germination and tillering, rather than tiller weight.
evidence: The claim is supported by tiller weight measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Benzoxazinoid soil conditioning increased biomass by promoting tiller density through enhanced germination and tillering, rather than tiller weight.
source: The weight of individual tillers was similar (Figure 5D), demonstrating that benzoxazinoid soil conditioning increased biomass by promoting tiller density, both through enhanced germination and tillering, rather than tiller weight.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that tiller density increased but individual tiller weight did not.

claim: Yield in both Claro and Fiorina was increased by 4–5% on benzoxazinoid conditioned soils.
source: Yield in both Claro and Fiorina was increased by 4–5% on benzoxazinoid conditioned soils (Figure 6A); the productivity of both varieties fell within the expected range of top-yielding winter wheat varieties in Switzerland (variety testing Agroscope).
evidence: The claim is supported by yield measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The productivity of both Claro and Fiorina varieties fell within the expected range of top-yielding winter wheat varieties in Switzerland.
source: Yield in both Claro and Fiorina was increased by 4–5% on benzoxazinoid conditioned soils (Figure 6A); the productivity of both varieties fell within the expected range of top-yielding winter wheat varieties in Switzerland (variety testing Agroscope).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with established knowledge about wheat variety performance in Switzerland.

claim: The number of kernels per tiller, the kernel weight per tiller and the thousand kernel weight did not differ between soil conditioning treatments.
source: The number of kernels per tiller, the kernel weight per tiller and the thousand kernel weight did not differ between soil conditioning treatments (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B), showing that the increase in yield is primarily the result of more kernels being produced per area.
evidence: The claim is supported by kernel measurements shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The increase in yield is primarily the result of more kernels being produced per area.
source: The number of kernels per tiller, the kernel weight per tiller and the thousand kernel weight did not differ between soil conditioning treatments (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B), showing that the increase in yield is primarily the result of more kernels being produced per area.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that yield increased but individual kernel parameters did not change.

claim: Volume per weight, kernel surface area, kernel length and kernel width were not affected by soil conditioning.
source: Volume per weight, kernel surface area, kernel length and kernel width were not affected by soil conditioning (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by kernel morphology measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: Kernel quality and baking quality were high and showed no differences between soil conditioning treatments.
source: Kernel quality and baking quality were high and showed no differences between soil conditioning treatments (Figure 6C–E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by kernel quality measurements shown in Figures 6C–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: No benzoxazinoid conditioning effects were found on micronutrient content in wheat kernels.
source: No benzoxazinoid conditioning effects were found (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by micronutrient measurements shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Maize benzoxazinoid soil conditioning increases wheat yield without affecting kernel quality.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that maize benzoxazinoid soil conditioning increases wheat yield without affecting kernel quality.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined observations of increased yield and unchanged kernel quality parameters.

claim: Maize plants releasing benzoxazinoids can improve plant growth and crop yield via plant-soil feedbacks under agronomically realistic conditions.
source: Here, we demonstrate that maize plants releasing benzoxazinoids can improve plant growth and crop yield via plant-soil feedbacks under agronomically realistic conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing improved wheat performance following benzoxazinoid-producing maize.

claim: Benzoxazinoid soil conditioning by the preceding crop increased subsequent wheat emergence, tillering and plant performance in the field, resulting in higher plant biomass and kernel yield.
source: We found that benzoxazinoid soil conditioning by the preceding crop increased subsequent wheat emergence, tillering and plant performance in the field, resulting in higher plant biomass and kernel yield.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results across multiple phenotypes.

claim: Weed cover was unaffected by benzoxazinoid soil conditioning.
source: Because weed cover was unaffected, and increased insect infestation did not result in increased leave damage, we conclude that the positive effects on yield were the result of directly improved germination and tillering rather than changes in plant competition or pest damage.
evidence: The claim is supported by weed cover measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Increased insect infestation did not result in increased leaf damage.
source: Because weed cover was unaffected, and increased insect infestation did not result in increased leave damage, we conclude that the positive effects on yield were the result of directly improved germination and tillering rather than changes in plant competition or pest damage.
evidence: The claim is supported by leaf damage measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The positive effects on yield were the result of directly improved germination and tillering rather than changes in plant competition or pest damage.
source: Because weed cover was unaffected, and increased insect infestation did not result in increased leave damage, we conclude that the positive effects on yield were the result of directly improved germination and tillering rather than changes in plant competition or pest damage.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that yield increased while weed cover and leaf damage did not change significantly.

claim: The observed increase in biomass is different from what was observed in an earlier greenhouse study.
source: Interestingly, the observed increase in biomass is different from what was observed in an earlier greenhouse study (Cadot et al., 2021a).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with results from a cited study.

claim: The discrepancy between field and greenhouse results is partially explained by the fact that the greenhouse study investigated individual plant performance and did not take into account germination effects.
source: This discrepancy is partially explained by the fact that the greenhouse study investigated individual plant performance and did thus not take into account germination effects.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing the current study design with the cited greenhouse study.

claim: The identity of the preceding crop is known to affect growth, tiller density, yield, and kernel protein content of wheat.
source: In crop rotations the identity of the preceding crop is known to affect growth, tiller density, yield, and kernel protein content of wheat (Anderson, 2008; Rieger et al., 2008; Sieling and Christen, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The release of chemicals by the preceding crop is sufficient to enhance overall crop yield through enhanced germination and tillering.
source: Our work expands this knowledge by demonstrating that the release of chemicals by the preceding crop is sufficient to enhance overall crop yield through enhanced germination and tillering.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing benzoxazinoid-dependent effects.

claim: Higher plant densities are often associated with lower grain quality.
source: Although higher plant densities are often associated with lower grain quality (Bastos et al., 2020), we found that the yield increase did not affect physical parameters, grain micronutrient composition, grain quality, and baking quality.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The yield increase did not affect physical parameters, grain micronutrient composition, grain quality, and baking quality.
source: Although higher plant densities are often associated with lower grain quality (Bastos et al., 2020), we found that the yield increase did not affect physical parameters, grain micronutrient composition, grain quality, and baking quality.
evidence: The claim is supported by kernel quality measurements shown in Figures 6B-F and supplements.

claim: The increase in yield of 4–5% is equivalent to more than two years of breeding.
source: The increase in yield of 4–5% is equivalent to more than two years of breeding (Le Gouis et al., 2020), and represents a true advantage because quality remained constant without additional agricultural inputs.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with breeding progress rates from a cited study.

claim: The yield increase represents a true advantage because quality remained constant without additional agricultural inputs.
source: The increase in yield of 4–5% is equivalent to more than two years of breeding (Le Gouis et al., 2020), and represents a true advantage because quality remained constant without additional agricultural inputs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that yield increased without quality changes or additional inputs.

claim: Benzoxazinoid exudation and responsiveness to benzoxazinoid soil conditioning are promising targets for future breeding efforts.
source: Benzoxazinoid exudation and responsiveness to benzoxazinoid soil conditioning are thus promising targets for future breeding efforts.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed benefits of benzoxazinoid conditioning.

claim: Benzoxazinoids alter the composition of root-associated microbes.
source: In line with previous studies, we found benzoxazinoids alter the composition of root-associated microbes (Hu et al., 2018b; Cotton et al., 2019; Kudjordjie et al., 2019; Cadot et al., 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by the current study's data (Figure 2) and citations to prior research.

claim: Benzoxazinoid effects on microbial communities disappeared by the end of the vegetative growth of the next crop.
source: However, these effects disappeared by the end of the vegetative growth of the next crop.
evidence: The claim is supported by microbial community analysis during wheat growth shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The benzoxazinoid chemical fingerprint persisted across both cultivation periods.
source: By contrast, the benzoxazinoid chemical fingerprint persisted across both cultivation periods.
evidence: The claim is supported by benzoxazinoid measurements shown in Figures 1A-C.

claim: AMPO is a microbial degradation product with a half life of months.
source: AMPO, a microbial degradation product with a half life of months (Macías et al., 2004; Niemeyer, 2009), was found in higher concentrations in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils of all three wheat varieties.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research on AMPO properties.

claim: AMPO was found in higher concentrations in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils of all three wheat varieties.
source: AMPO, a microbial degradation product with a half life of months (Macías et al., 2004; Niemeyer, 2009), was found in higher concentrations in benzoxazinoid conditioned soils of all three wheat varieties.
evidence: The claim is supported by benzoxazinoid measurements during wheat growth shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The benzoxazinoid chemical fingerprint is more long-lived than the change in the microbial fingerprint.
source: Thus, we conclude that the benzoxazinoid chemical fingerprint is more long-lived that the change in the microbial fingerprint.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that chemical differences persisted while microbial differences did not.

claim: Microbial community changes may still have contributed to plant-soil feedback effects, as many of the late phenotypes were explained by initial differences in germination and tillering.
source: Microbial community changes may still have contributed to plant-soil feedback effects, as many of the late phenotypes (Figure 5, Figure 6) were explained by initial differences in germination and tillering, where transient microbiome effects could still have been stronger.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference about the timing of effects.

claim: This study presents a proof of concept for the utilization of plant root exuded metabolites to increase agricultural yield without additional external inputs.
source: This study presents a proof of concept for the utilization of plant root exuded metabolites to increase agricultural yield without additional external inputs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing yield increases without additional inputs.

claim: The findings open new avenues to optimize plant traits in crop rotations for a more sustainable agriculture.
source: Our findings open new avenues to optimize plant traits in crop rotations for a more sustainable agriculture.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the implications of the study's findings.

claim: The field experiment was conducted in two phases: the conditioning phase with maize and the feedback phase with wheat.
source: The field experiment was conducted in two phases, the conditioning phase with maize (Zea mays) and the feedback phase with wheat (Triticum aestivum, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design as documented in the methods and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The wild type maize inbred line W22 and the benzoxazinoid-deficient bx1 transposon knockout mutant were used in the conditioning phase.
source: The wild type maize inbred line W22 and the benzoxazinoid-deficient bx1 transposon knockout mutant (gene identifier GRMZM2G085381; Ds, B.W06.0775) (Tzin et al., 2015) were kindly provided by Georg Jander (Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; USA).
evidence: The claim describes the plant materials used, with citation support for the mutant.

claim: CH Claro, Fiorina, and Sailor are commonly cultivated wheat varieties in Switzerland.
source: All three wheat varieties were provided by Saatzucht Düdingen (Düdingen; Switzerland) and are commonly cultivated in Switzerland (recommended varieties by Agroscope).
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about wheat variety cultivation in Switzerland.

claim: Claro is an obligate winter wheat.
source: Claro is an obligate winter wheat, Fiorina can be cultivated as winter or spring wheat, and Sailor is a common forage winter wheat variety.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about wheat variety characteristics.

claim: Fiorina can be cultivated as winter or spring wheat.
source: Claro is an obligate winter wheat, Fiorina can be cultivated as winter or spring wheat, and Sailor is a common forage winter wheat variety.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about wheat variety characteristics.

claim: Sailor is a common forage winter wheat variety.
source: Claro is an obligate winter wheat, Fiorina can be cultivated as winter or spring wheat, and Sailor is a common forage winter wheat variety.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about wheat variety characteristics.

claim: The experiment was carried out in 2019 and 2020 on a field at the Agroscope research station in Posieux, Switzerland.
source: The experiment was carried out in 2019 and 2020 on a field at the Agroscope research station in Posieux, Switzerland (parcel 2.3, 46°46′23.09″N 7°06′22.95″E).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental location and timing.

claim: The soil was classified as a sandy loam.
source: The soil was classified as a sandy loam.
evidence: The claim describes a soil property determined through classification.

claim: There was a long-lasting drought period in spring 2020 during the feedback phase.
source: There was a long-lasting drought period in spring 2020 (feedback phase).
evidence: The claim describes an environmental condition during the experiment.

claim: Chickweed (Stellaria media), Persian speedwell (Veronica persica), and Shepherd's purse (Capsella bursa-pastoris) were the most abundant weeds.
source: Chickweed (Stellaria media), Persian speedwell (Veronica persica), and Shepherd's purse (Capsella bursa-pastoris) were the most abundant weeds.
evidence: The claim is based on weed identification and abundance observations.

claim: The main herbivore that occurred in the field was the cereal leaf beetle Oulema melanopus.
source: The main herbivore that occurred in the field was the cereal leaf beetle Oulema melanopus.
evidence: The claim is based on insect identification and abundance observations.

claim: Benzoxazinoids are a class of indole-derived secondary metabolites that are produced and released in high quantities by important food crops such as maize and wheat.
source: Benzoxazinoids are a class of indole-derived secondary metabolites that are produced and released in high quantities by important food crops such as maize and wheat (Frey et al., 2009; Hu et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about benzoxazinoids, supported by citations.

claim: Multiple functions of benzoxazinoids have been described, ranging from defense to nutrient uptake.
source: Multiple functions of benzoxazinoids have been described, ranging from defense to nutrient uptake (Niemeyer, 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about benzoxazinoids, supported by a citation.

claim: Soil conditioning by benzoxazinoids can feed back on growth and defense of maize and wheat, where the strength and direction of the feedback depend on the plant genotype and soil characteristics.
source: Soil conditioning by benzoxazinoids can feed back on growth and defense of maize and wheat, where the strength and direction of the feedback depend on the plant genotype and soil characteristics (Hu et al., 2018b; Cadot et al., 2021a).
evidence: The claim is based on prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Benzoxazinoids can shape root microbial communities.
source: Benzoxazinoids can shape root microbial communities (Hu et al., 2018b; Cotton et al., 2019; Kudjordjie et al., 2019; Cadot et al., 2021b), chelate iron in the soil and possibly reduce the performance of non-benzoxazinoid producing plants via allelopathic effects (Bigler et al., 1996; Niemeyer, 2009; Hu et al., 2018a).
evidence: The claim is based on prior research, supported by citations.
